claim: A scheme is a defeasible premise-conclusion template with a fixed list of critical questions (CQs); the conclusion stands until a CQ gets a good answer against it. Walton, Reed and Macagno list about 60 main schemes (96 in the compendium).
agent_test: Build a CQ table per scheme in code; check that the S4 test list is driven by scheme type, not by free generation.

claim: Zero-shot LLMs write poor critical questions: on a 220-intervention debate benchmark the best of 11 models scored about 56 on a useful-question score, and prompt tuning, few-shot and fine-tuning barely moved it. In the shared task the best system reached 67.6 only after human relabelling.
agent_test: At equal tokens, compare plain 'list objections' against scheme-CQ prompting on our own items; score by a reference-matched check, not a model grade.

claim: Direct LLM labelling of whether a CQ is useful agrees with humans almost not at all (kappa <= 0.1); reference-matching judges reach kappa 0.40-0.57; human annotators themselves reach only 0.54.
agent_test: Never let the model grade its own CQs. Test a reference-matching or output-based check against a model grade.

claim: Putting scheme names, definitions and CQ templates into the prompt gives no consistent gain. It helped only when mixed with unconstrained prompts (Alicante: 62.4 vs 57.7 with judge), hurt when each scheme had its own prompt (51.6), and ARG2ST found no benefit. Template quality decides the effect. Gap search added: COGNAC validation 0.83 (retrieved examples) vs 0.81 (plus schemes) and 0.79 vs 0.82 (annotated examples without vs with schemes); ARG2ST found scheme labels worst of all prompts; Webis dropped scheme prompts. Still no test at equal tokens on answer accuracy, only on question quality.
agent_test: Run three arms at equal tokens: free CQs, scheme CQs, mixed. Keep scheme CQs only if mixed beats free.

claim: LLM-written CQs cover things the Walton templates lack: only 25% (52 of 207) of valid LLM CQs matched a theory CQ, and 16% asked for definitions, a type no template lists. But only 28% of 495 raw LLM CQs were relevant and valid (2023 13B models).
agent_test: Add a 'definition of terms' CQ to the generic list and test whether it finds errors the scheme list misses.

claim: Walton templates are not turnkey: 39.44% of instantiated template questions needed manual editing, and four ER schemes had no definitions, so filling them confused models (dropping them lifted useful from 68.28 to 72.22).
agent_test: Hand-write CQ lists for the 5 to 8 schemes we use; do not auto-instantiate all 60.

claim: A generate-many-then-select step helps little: an LLM judge picked 3.4 points more useful questions than random (p<0.05), while an oracle gained 34.2 points. Most of the gap is not closed. Gap search added: a small trained reranker (ModernBERT) on 6 candidates raised the Webis test score from 0.49 to 0.57 (manual relabel; validation-only reranker 0.48), whereas LLM judges said Useful to 8.4 of 10 questions with only 44.4% truly useful (TriLLaMA) and debate or deliberation judging did not help (52.0 and 37.3 vs 53.9). A trained selector helps; an LLM judge mostly does not.
agent_test: Select by code-run checks or a small trained selector, not a model judge; measure how much a code selector closes the oracle gap (still unmeasured).

claim: Scheme classification: trained annotators agree substantially (kappa 0.723 on 60 Walton schemes, 0.61 with the full guideline set); LLMs reach only F1 0.65 at best on real Kialo arguments; the same models are near perfect (0.98-0.99) on machine-written textbook arguments; classifiers collapse on real dialogue (F1 1.0 to 44.8 on QT30). Cause to effect and expert opinion are the most misclassified.
agent_test: Do not rely on the model to name the scheme. Route by cheap cues, or run the generic CQ list plus the 2 to 3 CQs of the most likely scheme; test scheme-routing accuracy.

claim: Fallacy and scheme classifiers learn which scheme an argument uses, not whether it is used correctly: a fine-tuned classifier flags 16.6% of native valid items but 58.9% of scheme-matched valid items (Reddit-trained: 5.7% to 62.0%); on human-confirmed valid items the false-positive rate was 56.6% (30 of 53).
agent_test: A CQ check must test the content (is the cited expert real, is the case similar), not the form. Run on scheme-matched valid vs invalid items.

claim: Prompting pipelines built on critical questions lift LLM answers over direct and chain-of-thought baselines: ArgMed-Agents on MedQA (GPT-3.5 52.7 to 62.1; GPT-4 67.8 to 83.3, 300 items) and CQoT on MT-Bench (+4.61% reasoning, +5.4% math, five models). Neither compared with token-matched best-of-N, and CQoT uses generic, not per-scheme, CQs. Gap search added: no study isolates a CQ step against best-of-N, but general critique-vs-voting work shows model-run critique loses to majority vote at equal calls unless the budget is large (see K23).
agent_test: Equal-token comparison: CQ-test step vs best-of-N vs plain, on 1 to 2 of our benchmarks (G7).

claim: In CQoT, dropping the CQ step (plan only) lands between baseline and full pipeline (Llama reasoning 8.05, 8.3, 8.4; math 8.95, 9.25, 9.55), so the CQs add value beyond the plan. Authors suspect a model-size threshold near 70B (untested) and a latency of seconds to minutes.
agent_test: Ablate the CQ step alone at equal tokens; check small models separately.

claim: When asked to answer scheme CQs, LLMs lean to yes and fail on grounds and sufficiency: GPT-4 and Mixtral answered yes to 53.3% of negative CQs (fine-tuned RoBERTa 70.7 vs GPT-4 63.5 macro-F1); in 6,778 cells of moral-dilemma defence, 18.2% failed, 67.8% of them from two models (Sonnet 4.6, Llama 3.3). Gap search added: an LLM usefulness judge accepted 8.4 of 10 questions with 44.4% really useful (TriLLaMA); ChatGPT agrees with a restated fact in yes/no form (CoVe); compliance with invalid arguments ranges 0.2% to 95% by model (Big-Big-SycoBench); judges detect absence at 0.50-0.63 vs presence at 0.79-0.94.
agent_test: Make CQ answers a forced choice with a quoted passage, and verify by code where possible; measure yes-bias on seeded-wrong arguments.

claim: Models change scheme between reasoning and justification (on about 1 in 5 dilemmas) and collapse to one scheme (value-based practical reasoning, about 72% and 67%). Reasoning-track defence beats justification-track by only 0.02 to 0.04 normalised.
agent_test: Do not trust the model's stated scheme; use the scheme only as a routing label that code assigns.

claim: LLM scheme-based analysis is stable across models and runs for clear cases (fable: 100 of 100 green, stability 1.00) and diverges for ambiguous ones; named failures are source-ungrounded inference, CQs with no supporting passage and role inversion.
agent_test: Require a verbatim quote for each premise; code rejects CQ answers with no quote.

claim: Lay people use scheme-specific criteria (expertise and trustworthiness for authority; relevant similarity for analogy; sufficiency of cause for cause-to-effect) when judging arguments, but a qualitative study coded by scheme-aware analysts cannot show these criteria raise accuracy.
agent_test: Do not claim CQs improve judgement because people use them; test on the agent.

claim: Statistical evidence persuades more than anecdotal or causal evidence, and lay people expect it to (ranking statistical > expert > causal > anecdotal); expectations and actual effects only partly match.
agent_test: Low value for the agent; use only as a prior that agents also over-weight numbers (test with seeded fake statistics).

claim: Argument from ignorance is not always a fallacy: people rate positive evidence above negative, weigh the amount of evidence and the audience's prior, and the pattern replicated with source reliability instead of study count (N=73, polarity F(1,72)=11.58; Exp 2 N=72). A Bayesian account fits.
agent_test: The CQ for absence of evidence should ask how thoroughly the evidence was searched; test with seeded thorough vs shallow searches.
audit: downgraded 2026-10-27 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: Whether bare expert-opinion arguments are weak is disputed: Mizrahi (2013) says the bare form 'E says p' barely raises probability; Walton, Seidel and Hinton reply that the full scheme with its 6 CQs is not bare. A Bayesian model of expertise and trustworthiness (Harris et al. 2016) is reported broadly in line with ratings but was only seen as an abstract.
agent_test: Test the 6 expert CQs against a single 'is this a consensus' question on seeded expert claims.

claim: Teaching with a CQ box in argument diagrams led students to add more CQ-linked refutations over time and transferred to an unprompted in-class essay but not to a take-home paper (quasi-experiment, one scheme, 3 sections, N not read).
agent_test: Weak; ignore for the agent.

claim: Zero-shot LLMs can match or beat fine-tuned fallacy classifiers out of domain, but results swing widely (GPT-4 macro-F1 Argotario 79.87 vs 72.38; ElecDeb 41.25 vs 62.37); zero-shot chain of thought was the most robust prompt.
agent_test: Fallacy detection is a different task; do not generalise to CQ testing.

claim: LLMs can write textbook instances of Walton schemes that humans mostly accept (89.1% of 4,000 kept; EN 74.8% valid after GPT-3.5), but classifiers trained on them do not transfer to real dialogue, so such corpora overstate real ability.
agent_test: Never evaluate scheme tools on generated arguments only.

claim: Without an outside signal, asking a model to critique and revise its own answer does not help and often hurts. A sound checker or tool does help, and most of the gain survives with the critique text removed: GPT-4 sound-verifier accuracy 8-87% vs LLM-as-critic 0-55% across four puzzle domains; CRITIC with tools +6.3 F1 over CoT on AmbigNQ vs about 0 without tools; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA fell 75.8 to 38.1 after self-correction.
agent_test: Judge each CQ with code or a tool where one exists; never accept a bare model re-read as the test.

claim: At equal calls or tokens, majority voting over samples beats model-run critique and debate, except at large budgets: GSM8K self-consistency 82.5/85.3/88.2 at 3/6/9 responses vs debate below it; a generative verifier needed about 8x compute to match self-consistency and 128x to gain 3.8 points on MATH; sampling plus a sound verifier matched critique.
agent_test: Run a CQ-test arm against best-of-N at equal tokens before keeping any CQ step; expect the CQ step to win mainly on hard items and on items without a votable answer.

claim: The format of a check changes whether flaws pass. Open questions answered in a fresh context beat yes/no questions that restate the claim (CoVe: 0.22 vs 0.19 vs 0.15 precision); models rarely flag flaws without an explicit instruction (premise critique 11.0% for GPT-4o unprompted vs 73-78% for others when told to check); judges find added content (0.79-0.94) far better than missing content (0.50-0.63), and a closed list-then-verify procedure recovered detection.
agent_test: Seeded-wrong test: compare open-quote-required vs yes/no CQ format, and a closed checklist for absence-type CQs, per model.

claim: There is no clean 70B threshold for CQ pipelines. Writing CQs: 8B to 405B gave +1.3 points (TriLLaMA), and 24B matched 70B (CriticalBrew). Judging flaws: small and medium models sit near chance on critique (CriticBench), 13B-scale self-verifiers are weak (Zhang), but open models were within 10% of frontier models on proof checking with more inconsistency (Naik). Reliability of the judge, not size alone, is the limit.
agent_test: Repeat each CQ check 3 times and keep only agreed verdicts; test the cheapest model that passes seeded-wrong checks.

claim: Cost: simple chain-of-thought gave most of the CQ-generation gain; tree of thoughts cost $21.10 vs $0.98 for zero-shot CoT per 30 runs (97.39M vs 2.17M input tokens) with no better score; multi-agent CQ generation gains followed agent count (more tokens).
agent_test: Always report tokens beside score for any CQ variant.

claim: In real debate data the schemes that occur are mostly example (175), practical reasoning (135), cause to effect (55) and consequences (38); analogy (11), expert opinion (10) and authority (4) are rare. Which schemes occur in ARC, BrainTeaser or novelty reasoning is unmeasured.
agent_test: Count scheme types in our own agent traces before building per-scheme lists; start with cause, example and practical reasoning plus a generic list.

claim: Walton wording can be coded for expert opinion (six questions: expertise, field, opinion, trustworthiness, consistency, backup evidence) and as short templates for analogy (similarity, relevant differences, known case sound) and cause (reliable link, interfering factors, correlation vs cause). The book itself was not opened, so the exact analogy and cause wording is unverified, and the 39.44% hand-edit rate means templates need slot filling and rewording.
agent_test: Code the three lists as slot templates, fill slots by code, and let the model reword only the question text.

claim: The public CQs-Gen leaderboard holds no retrievable 2026 frontier or reasoning-model scores (results dataset private); the only reasoning models run are DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-8B in one shared-task paper, as charts. Whether 2026 models still top out near 56 is unknown.
agent_test: Run recent models on the public validation set ourselves if CQ generation becomes central.
